title: The Sunday Essay: In Defence of Context
author: Leadership, Rewritten
summary: In this essay in his defence series, Claydon argues that personality instruments such as DiSC say little about any individual but can reveal a great deal about the organisation that uses them. Through Maya's observation that nearly every promotable leader in a cohort registered as Red, he shifts attention from the person to the environment that keeps rewarding that posture. He traces a contextual lineage from Marston, Freud and Jung through motive theory, Self-Determination Theory, Social Identity Theory and McAdams's narrative identity, to explain how environments pull differently on different people and stabilise particular selves. The practical conclusion is to treat personality data as an ecological clue, reading population patterns as hypotheses about culture, power and legitimacy rather than as verdicts on essence. It is a demanding but useful reframe for anyone running assessments or talent processes.
points: Trait psychology is a psychology of the stranger, and it is too thin to explain behaviour inside organisations with their own pressures, incentives and promotion logics.
When a whole promotable cohort clusters around one posture, the finding is about the organisation's adaptive grammar, not a timeless leadership type.
Environments that support or frustrate autonomy, competence and relatedness shape behaviour that is easily mistaken for temperament.
Organisations often misread themselves by assuming they reward what they say they value when the promotion pattern shows the posture actually legitimised.
Personality data is best used ecologically: look at selection, stabilisation and the stories that dignify a pattern before drawing any conclusion about people.
quotes: Weak instruments such as DiSC may tell very little about any one individual and still reveal something important at population level. If, inside a given organisation, the people who keep rising all cluster around the same broad posture — forceful, fast, active under pressure, inclined to meet ambiguity through counter-move rather than receptivity — then the important question is no longer whether the instrument has discovered a timeless leadership essence.

Yet, the pattern in the cohort suggested something else. However healthy the culture sounded in aspiration, the lived conditions appeared to reward people who could respond actively under contested conditions — people who could move decisively through ambiguity, absorb contest without paralysis, and remain credible in a system where advancement seemed to depend on proving one could master pressure rather than soften it.

A trait can tell that someone tends, on average, to be forceful, agreeable, emotionally steady, or imaginative. What it cannot tell nearly as well is how that person became viable in a given role, what a particular environment is pulling from them, what adaptations have become necessary under repeated pressure, or what kind of self a system keeps selecting for.

An organisation that repeatedly promotes active response under contested and ambiguous conditions may not simply be selecting “dominant personalities.” It may be rewarding a particular conversion of motive into behaviour: achievement expressed as forceful mastery, power expressed as decisive control, even affiliation expressed through loyalty to the dominant game.

They assume that what they are rewarding is universal leadership merit, when what they may actually be rewarding is conformity to a local identity code. Over time, the code becomes invisible because it looks natural. “Good leaders” are simply the people who already know how to sound and act the right way in this system.

It can show what kinds of behaviour are repeatedly rewarded, what kinds of adaptation survive contact with the system, and what forms of selfhood begin to look like common sense at senior levels. At that point, the organisation itself becomes the object of diagnosis.
The most serious use of personality at work, then, is ecological. It treats assessments as one imperfect source of evidence about how a system is functioning.
